User request:
Compare only delivery choices for a clickable product tour: real React controls must remain interactive for the viewer, yet I request only a standard MP4 file and no web app/link. Can Flute or Remotion preserve that interactivity in the MP4? I have zero hosting budget. Distinguish a filmed interaction from an interactive artifact; do not silently publish a web demo.

No real media, runtime, customers, revenue or performance results are supplied. Use only stated facts. Named media assets in requests are declared future inputs, not files decoded in this workspace.

answer:
**No. Neither Flute nor Remotion can preserve viewer-operated React controls in a standard MP4.** Your two delivery requirements—real controls remaining interactive and only an MP4 file—cannot both be satisfied.

An MP4 contains encoded picture and audio. It does not retain the React runtime, DOM, event handlers or application state. A viewer can pause or seek using their video player, but cannot operate the product controls pictured inside the video.

| Delivery choice | What the viewer receives | Real product controls remain clickable? | Hosting implications |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flute → MP4 | A filmed presentation of existing React components, potentially showing scripted interactions and camera movement | No | File delivery needs no web hosting |
| Remotion → MP4 | An authored, frame-driven React film showing predetermined interface states and actions | No | File delivery needs no web hosting; licence eligibility needs separate checking |
| Runnable interactive artifact | React code executing in a browser or suitable app runtime | Potentially, with implementation and verification | A local package could avoid paid hosting, but is an additional artifact outside your MP4-only requirement |

A **filmed interaction** shows a chosen sequence: a button is pressed, a panel opens, text changes. Those actions become pixels in the recording; every viewer watches the same sequence.

An **interactive artifact** lets the viewer choose the action and executes the corresponding logic. Even if a browser preview remains interactive during authoring, exporting that preview to MP4 removes that executable behavior. Adding clickable overlays in a special player would require a separate runtime and would not preserve the React controls inside the MP4 itself.

The supplied router records a Flute 0.1.2 browser-host pilot using genuine React panels and exporting an MP4. That supports filmed UI presentation within its tested scope, not arbitrary React compatibility or interactive video delivery. Its Remotion 4.0.535 pilot supports authored video export; React-component support is separately marked documented. Neither record establishes clickable controls in an exported MP4.

**For your exact requirements, neither tool is a qualifying delivery choice.** Zero hosting budget is compatible with distributing a passive MP4, but it does not change the format’s capabilities. There is no need to select a renderer or run an experiment to resolve this format conflict.

This is a comparison only. No demo was published, and no rendering or artifact QA was performed; real media and renderer runtimes are absent.

answer:
**No—we cannot promise this.** The supplied declarations already conflict with a reliable stream-copy join into one continuous MP4 video track; compatibility inspection would still be necessary even for matching declarations.

| Requirement | Copy-only assessment |
|---|---|
| H.264 clip-a + VP9 clip-b | Different codecs cannot be treated as one compatible stream by ordinary copy-only concatenation. Putting both in an MP4 container does not resolve that mismatch. |
| 1920×1080 + 1080×1920 | Different dimensions and orientations prevent a consistent picture format. Scaling, padding or cropping would require re-encoding. |
| 30 fps + 24 fps | Stream copy preserves encoded frames; it cannot promise uniform motion cadence. Frame-rate differences alone are not always fatal, but timestamps and playback compatibility need inspection. |
| Smooth cuts | Clean hard cuts depend on valid decoding boundaries and timestamps. Dissolves or other blended transitions require generating new frames, outside copy-only constraints. |
| Common score | A supplied, approved, MP4-compatible audio track might be muxed without encoding. Mixing, fades, looping or loudness processing generally require audio processing and encoding. No score or audio metadata is supplied. |

For the music layer, **video-first** fits: preserve picture timing and select an existing score against measured cut points. That remains conditional on actual durations, a suitable audio export, usage rights, and decisions about any original clip audio. A continuous score cannot fix incompatible video streams.

The router documents FFmpeg concatenation but does not establish a tested join for these inputs. Its retained audio-mux evidence concerns preserving an already compatible video stream, so it does not support this promise.

**Recommendation: keep the existing tools and report the requested result as unsupported under the stated constraints.** No new renderer or encoding action is warranted for this comparison.

No media was inspected or processed. Codec parameters, timebases, keyframes, timestamps, audio compatibility, seam playback, sync and final encoded-file checks remain blocked by absent files. Inspection could establish additional facts; it would not make the declared codec mismatch disappear.
